**2026-11-04.** **Senders see a new retryable refusal during a database problem:** a delivery with an explicit event id or a declared body-path `dedupKey` that can't be checked for a duplicate is now refused instead of processed unchecked. **It also closes a masking leak: in a flow that declares masking, the raw message and every inbound header, including credentials such as an API key, showed in audit, inspect and snapshots.** **It also stops a message on one owner's channel resuming another owner's draining instance.** This release also adds `bpmn-svg`, a standalone library that draws BPMN diagrams as SVG, and renews the image scan's time-boxed entries. There is no `urn:sutra:q:1.0` change, no archive format, deploymentId or snapshot format change, and no migration.

## Security: a message could resume another owner's draining instance

**What could happen.** A message on one owner's channel could resume an instance parked under another
owner's draining deployment. That instance then ran on, with the sender's payload, as if it had been
answered by its own owner. A session-ending message could also release the other owner's session the same
way. In the test that shows this, tenant `t1`'s message completed tenant `t2`'s instance and the sender got
a normal `200`.

**The conditions, all at once:**

- Two owners, a different tenant or module, share one engine.
- The other owner's deployment is draining: replaced or undeployed, with an instance still parked.
- A wait in that deployment subscribes to a channel with the same name as the channel the message came in
  on.
- The message's correlation value matches the alias that instance parked on.

A deployment on an engine with a single owner isn't affected.

**Since when.** Every public release from `v0.2.0-rc.1` to `v0.6.16`. That comes from reading the source of
those tags, where the fallback takes every draining deployment with no owner check. The defect was only run
on the code just before this fix.

**What changed.** A message only falls back to draining deployments with the same tenant and module labels as
its channel's deployment. A message that matches nothing gets the same error as any message that correlates to
nothing. A parked older version of the same owner still resumes after a newer one takes the route.

**A change for packages with no labels.** A package missing its `tenant` or `module` label has no owner to
compare, so it no longer falls back at all. An instance parked under such a package stops correlating once
the package is replaced. Give packages both labels before you upgrade them.

**What to do.** On a multi-owner engine, check your audit trail for instances of a draining deployment that
resumed from a channel of another deployment. The engine records no field that says so directly, so look for
resumes of an old deployment you didn't expect.

## Security: the raw message and inbound headers leaked past masking

**What leaked.** `event.body` holds the raw inbound message, and `event.headers` and `header` hold every
inbound header, including `X-Api-Key` and `Authorization`. In a flow that declares masking, with
`<q:redactors>` on a `q:source` or a `sensitive` payload variable, only the payload variable was masked.
These were not:

| Surface | What it showed |
|---|---|
| `<q:audit capture="payload">` output | The raw body and headers in clear. |
| The inspect API, `GET /sutra/instances/{id}` | The raw body and headers in clear. |
| The stored snapshot, `instance_state` | The raw body and headers unencrypted, even with a master key set. |

Running the unfixed code showed all three in a flow with a `sensitive` payload and a master key. The
`<q:redactors>` case comes from reading the same code paths, and is covered by a tier-1 test of the fix.

**Since when.** From reading the source of the published tags, the same code is in every public release
from `v0.2.0-rc.1` to `v0.6.16`. Only the code just before this fix was actually run, so older releases
are by reading, not by test.

**What changed, for a flow that declares masking.** Its source now also stores masked copies of `event`
and `header`. In those, `body`, every header value, the CloudEvent attributes and the dedup key are masked
whole; header names stay. Audit and inspect show the copies, and `event` and `header` are encrypted in the
snapshot when a master key is set.

The flow still reads the real values, so routing, `q:alias`, `dedupKey`, inbound auth and tracing work as
before. An alias built from a masked value now shows as masked in the audit trail.

**Flows that declare no masking are unchanged: their inbound headers and body, including API keys, still
reach audit (with `capture="payload"`), inspect and the snapshot in clear.** To avoid that:

- Declare masking on the flow: a `sensitive` payload variable is enough, and needs no redactor.
- Set a master key (`sutra.crypto.master-key`), or snapshots stay unencrypted even with masking.
- Avoid `capture="payload"` on a flow that doesn't declare masking.
- Limit who can reach the inspect API and the database.
- Or remove credentials before the engine: end authentication at a gateway that strips the header.

**What this doesn't cover:**

- With no master key, snapshots stay unencrypted, as a masked payload's always have.
- A `q:alias` value is stored in clear in `alias_index`, and isn't masked on the inspect API. So an alias
  built from a header holds that header's value.
- An explicit event id is stored in clear in `inbox_seen`.
- The trace id from `traceparent` is stored in clear with an outbound send, because tracing needs it.
- A copy of the body in another variable isn't masked unless that variable is `sensitive`. Lint now warns
  about this, below.
- Raw payload captured with a dead-letter incident wasn't reviewed.

**What to do about data already written:**

- **Audit records:** treat anything written with `capture="payload"` by a flow that declares masking as
  holding the raw message. This release doesn't rewrite it. Apply your own retention or redaction to those
  audit files, tables or exports.
- **Snapshots of instances parked before you upgrade:** these are not fixed by upgrading. Such an instance
  keeps showing the old raw body and headers and storing them unencrypted, until a later delivery to it replaces
  `event` and `header` on a source that declares masking. To clear them, let them finish or cancel them. Finished
  instances keep their stored row until `sutra.instance.retention` removes it, 7 days by default.
- **Database backups and replicas** of those tables hold the same data.
- **Rotate any credential sent as an inbound header to a flow on these surfaces.** That applies to flows
  that declared masking and to ones that didn't. Anyone who could read audit output, the inspect API, the
  database or its backups could read it.
- If raw messages held other secrets, treat those as exposed to the same people.

**New lint warnings, in a flow that declares masking.** Neither fails a build in this release. **The first
becomes an error in a later release.**

- `SUTRA.CONFIG.BPMN.RAW_BODY_UNMASKED`: a variable holds raw `event.body` text and isn't `sensitive`.
- `SUTRA.CONFIG.BPMN.RAW_BODY_STORED`: raw `event.body` text is written to a data store. Store columns
  have no at-rest encryption.

The lint follows assignments within one process. It doesn't follow a value into a store and out in another
process.

## Changed: what senders see during a database problem

- **A delivery with an explicit event id or a declared `dedupKey="body.<path>"` is never processed
  without its duplicate check.** It used to fail open: when the check failed, the delivery ran with no duplicate protection and left no
  record, so a redelivery ran again. It is now refused with
  `SUTRA.INBOUND.DEDUP_CHECK_UNAVAILABLE`, nothing runs, and a retry with the same id is safe. **This
  includes flows that don't otherwise touch the database, which used to keep answering during an
  outage and now answer `503`.**

  | Transport | What happens |
  |---|---|
  | HTTP | `503` with a problem document carrying the code. There's no `Retry-After` header. |
  | Dapr, Knative | `500`, which the sender's own retry policy treats as retryable. |
  | RabbitMQ | `basic.nack(requeue=true)`. |
  | AMQP 1.0 | The delivery is released, so the broker redelivers it. |
  | Kafka | The consumer seeks back to the record, so the next poll reads it again. |
  | SQS | The message stays in flight, and returns after its visibility timeout. |
  | Pub/Sub | The message is nacked, and redelivered after its ack deadline. |
  | File | The file moves back to the spool root for a later poll. |
  | `local://` hops | Retried with the outbox's backoff. |

- **A retry during a synchronous-call chain is now refused, not answered as a duplicate.** While a
  chain still holds an event's record, its outcome isn't known, so a repeat gets
  `SUTRA.INBOUND.DEDUP_IN_DOUBT`, with the same retry behaviour as above. A sender used to get a
  duplicate's normal answer. The refusal ends when the chain ends. **If the chain's process is gone, or
  it failed and couldn't release the record, it lasts until the sweep releases it: up to 15 minutes by
  default (`sutra.instance.inflight-chain-max-age`).**
- **A delivery with neither isn't refused.** It never reaches the check, and a repeat of it is a new
  delivery. On queue transports only the engine's own outbox key counts as an explicit id, so a message
  from another producer proceeds unless its flow declares a `dedupKey`.

## Fixed

- **`tc_outbox_relay_recovers_from_a_postgres_crash_mid_flight` no longer fails intermittently.** The
  known issue listed in 0.6.16 was the fail-open check described above. Locally the test failed 5 of 10
  runs before this release, and passed 10 of 10 after it, with no change to the test. In all 10 runs
  every accepted order called back.
- **A failed synchronous-call chain could delete an earlier delivery's dedup record,** so a third
  delivery ran as new. A chain now writes its keys in one transaction with its in-flight marker, and
  releases only keys it wrote. A key that's already recorded stops the chain before it makes a call.
- **A record a failed chain couldn't release could swallow a redelivery as a duplicate,** losing it.
  The chain's marker now stays until the sweep releases both, and a redelivery is refused and retried
  meanwhile.

## Added

- **`bpmn-svg` 0.1.0, a new library crate.** It draws BPMN 2.0 process diagrams as self-contained SVG
  from files with no BPMN-DI, using a layered auto-layout. Its only dependency is `quick-xml`, and it
  uses no other crate from this workspace, so other projects can use it alone.
  - `bpmn_svg::parse` reads standard BPMN into a small model and ignores BPMN-DI and vendor extensions.
  - `bpmn_svg::render` draws that model. The same input always gives byte-identical SVG.
  - The `css_variables` option writes each colour as a CSS variable, so a page can follow its light
    and dark themes. The default output is unchanged.

  The release workflow publishes it to crates.io alongside `sutra-feel` and `sutra-dmn`. See its
  [README](https://github.com/startr-trade/sutra/blob/main/rust/crates/bpmn-svg/README.md).

## Also changed

- `sutra docgen` draws its diagrams through `bpmn-svg`. It still parses with the engine's own loader,
  so its pages keep showing what the engine loads. Every `.bpmn` file in this repository regenerates
  byte-identical SVG.
- `.trivyignore.yaml` is renewed to 2026-12-09 after a re-triage of all 46 entries against the
  0.6.17 engine binary. None could be dropped, and the base image digest is unchanged:
  - The current `cc-debian12` digest ships the same `tzdata` and `libssl3` as the pinned one, so it
    clears nothing, and it adds one `ca-certificates` finding the pinned digest doesn't have.
  - Six `libssl3` entries said Debian had no fix. Debian now has one, which reaches this image only
    when the distroless base is rebuilt. The engine never loads `libssl3`, and the entries now say so.
  - The `glibc` and other entries that gave no reason now give one. The engine does import `regcomp`,
    `regexec` and `sscanf` through the bundled Kafka client and other C code, so those entries now say
    what keeps the flaws out of reach. The engine doesn't read the base image's `tzdata`: its time-zone
    rules are compiled into the binary.
